chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: The camp men loved him: food saved for the pianist and manly affection
summary: Playing piano won him affection, saved food from the cooks and a lifted spirit; he explains the hand-slap greeting as brotherhood.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Yes. But you were saying that they loved you, and they loved you because you played piano and that made you popular with them.

That was one of the main reasons, yes. It had to be first, and naturally my talent to play piano made people feel good. Well, it was a combination of two things to me, because see, if someone's complimenting you, that makes you smile and feel good, so you automatically give to them.

In other words that's-- I think that's one of the theories of christianity, although all these things are debatable. But there is much truth in it's better to give than receive. Because if you give in many instances, you will receive double.

You see what I mean, giving out my music that people complimented me, and they did things for me like all of the chefs. I never had to worry about grabbing this food, that's what I was trying to get around to telling you.
I didn't have to worry about this, when they found out that I played the piano, because they would save my food for me.
Because they liked to hear me play the piano.
You see? And it was this compensation that went on and started my career. As I said, in the army as a company clerk.

And actually I went from zero on the thermometer to the top of the thermometer, with my inspirations. Because when I left home I was down to the bottom in spirit, I left with my head hanging down and just like a little alley dog, you know, with his tail curled under. Let me get out of town in a hurry. You know what I mean?

And immediately my spirit was picked up completely, because I was surrounded by people who loved me and guys were happy and all men, and that's another thing, you see. There's something about men loving eachother that is different. I don't mean this --

I'm talking about manly love where another man loves you as a man, and grabs your hand, hey, man how are you feeling. Hey, how are you, baby, as they say now around, you know, hey baby, you know, hey, how's everything, you know, one of those things. You know what I mean?
You see, there's something about that that makes you great. So you see, (unintelligible) come on,
hey, baby, give me some skin. You know what they do, see, these are things that people don't know what they think that -- people are crazy.

See, after they're hitting the hands, like this together, hey, For instance you see (unintelligible) at the basketball games, at the football games. They come and introduce them, they hit eachother's hand like that, you know.
See? These are the things of course -- some people might consider this to be an illiterate way of expressing yourself, but it shows something.
No, I think it usually registers myself. I think it registers for what it is.
I think people can see that well, I mean you see that there's lots of people that try to pick up on those habits out there. Huh?
I like the way you say pick up on those habits.
That pick up is a very, very famous saying too.
It has many meanings about pick up.
